Intro
Now that the money-note MVP's core features are done, is the UI just going to stay like this forever?

Of course not. So today we're going to use Anthropic's official Frontend Design plugin to turn the bare-bones screens we built earlier into something more distinctive that looks like a real, production-grade product.

why-is-ais-default-design-taste-so-average
Why is AI's default design taste so average?
The biggest problem here is really "what the AI was trained on."
Why does that matter? Because AI learns by training on huge amounts of data, and the screens you're getting right now are basically the "average" of all that training data.
So by default, the AI's best strategy is to give you exactly the kind of screen you're looking at right now.
So how do we fix it? In UI design, there's one thing that matters a lot:
strong
"personality"
(and no, I don't mean a Quirk from My Hero Academia).
With that in mind, let's keep going!

the-makeover-talk-about-the-feel-not-css
The makeover: talk about the feel, not CSS
Before we start, let's look at the current screen so we can do a Before & After comparison:
Screenshot: money-note before the makeover
https://images.israynotarray.com/blog/ai/ithome-2026-vibe-coding/20260822200121.png

This makeover is going to touch a lot of places, since we're basically redoing the whole layout. So I strongly recommend using Plan Mode. That way it lays out the makeover plan first, and you only run it once you've confirmed it looks right.

When describing the UI, you can skip CSS entirely, but you do need to turn that feeling into design constraints you can actually check. That's how Frontend Design can build the screen you have in mind. Here's a prompt I used for reference:
language-txt shiki shiki-themes github-light github-light github-dark-high-contrast

Please call and use the frontend-design skill. First read SPEC.md and get familiar with the current components, then propose a UI update plan.

Product direction: a warm-toned paper ledger. Quiet, clean, numbers first. Not a generic blue-and-white admin dashboard.

Design constraints:
- Page background #F3EFE7, cards #FFFDF8, text #1F2925, secondary text #56625C
- Primary action #245C4A, accent #9A4F20, error #962E2E
- Use the system Traditional Chinese fonts, don't load remote fonts; no gradients, glass effects, emoji icons, or over-the-top shadows
- The home page needs a header area, a summary of this month's total spending and number of entries, tabs, the expense form, and the expense list
- Besides the pie chart, the stats page needs category names, amounts, and percentages as text, not relying on color alone
- Every input, select, and button is at least 44px tall, with visible labels and keyboard focus
- No horizontal scrolling at 375px; at 768px and up, content max width is 780px
- Support prefers-reduced-motion

Boundaries: keep the existing data structures and features. Only adjust markup structure and styles, and don't add any UI libraries.

In the plan, list the files that will change, the purpose of each file, and a review checklist for both features and screens after the changes.

When you're done, tell me which design decisions you made and why.

Letting the AI think it through
https://images.israynotarray.com/blog/ai/ithome-2026-vibe-coding/20260822204139.png
If you're a total beginner, your first reaction to this prompt is probably:
"Huh? That's way too complicated. How could I ever write something like that?"
I know this prompt looks pretty scary, but if you break it apart, it's really just the answers to these five questions. And I'm sure you can answer all five:
ul
li
What feel do you want?

That's the opening line, "a warm-toned paper ledger. Quiet, clean, numbers first." Just describe it the way you would to a friend, like "I want that warm feeling of a handwritten ledger, not something that looks like a company's internal admin system."
What absolutely has to be on the screen?
Name every "must-have" on the home page and the stats page one by one, so the AI doesn't redesign the important stuff out of existence.
What do you hate?
This one's actually the most important. The AI's default bundle is gradients, glass effects, over-the-top shadows, and so on. If you don't explicitly say "no," it'll assume you want them.
How small a screen does it need to work on?

Give it a phone width (375px is roughly the width of an iPhone screen) and basic tappability (buttons shouldn't be too small to hit). Otherwise it'll look great on your computer and break on your phone.
What's off-limits?
We're just giving the app new clothes, not performing surgery. So be clear that data and features can't be touched, or the screen gets prettier while the expense tracking breaks completely.
"So... what about colors like
? How am I supposed to know those?"
Honestly, you don't have to write it like I did. You can just tell the AI:
I want the feel of a warm-toned paper ledger. Please give me some color palettes for reference.
That's another technique you can use. In the end, all you need to say is "this is the feel I want" or "this color is too cool-toned, make it a bit warmer," and let the AI pick the rest.
So do you need to really know CSS or design? Basically, no. You just need to answer those five questions, and Frontend Design fills in the rest of the design knowledge.

That doesn't mean you can get away with knowing nothing about CSS or design. You still need some basics, otherwise how would you know whether what the AI made looks good? What I mean is that you can have a shot at a good-looking screen without spending time designing it yourself.

iterating-on-the-details-design-by-conversation
Iterating on the details: design by conversation

Even though the updated screens already look way better than before, the first version usually still needs some tweaking. "Taste" is subjective, after all, and there might be a few spots that just bug you, like...
Why is this number so small?
Why does this button look like that?
That's when you move into the "iterating on the details" stage.
This stage is pretty simple: get the screen to where you're mostly happy with it, then slowly polish the small stuff.

But when you're tweaking, don't just say something vague like "make it more refined," because the AI has no idea what "refined" means to you. Be clear about which element and what you want it to become, like...

Make the "This month's total spending" number a bit bigger. It's the most important information on the whole page.
Keep the current colors for the category tags, don't add any new colors.
Don't change the size of the delete button, just turn it warning red on mouse hover.
Make the "This month's total spending" number a bit bigger. It's the most important information on the whole page.
Keep the current colors for the category tags, don't add any new colors.
Don't change the size of the delete button, just turn it warning red on mouse hover.
Don't dump a whole pile on it at once. When tweaking, usually stick to a few points:
Only mention 2–3 things
Look at the result first
Then decide whether to tweak more
Then keep going until you're happy with it. The process is like going back and forth on revisions with a designer, except this designer won't give you a dramatic, baroque-level eye-roll lol.
But what if something "just looks off somehow," and you can't put your finger on why? There's a trick I want to share that you can try:
Take a screenshot of the screen, hand it back to the AI, and ask it to help analyze it.
When you hand it over, though, you still need to mention a few key points:

This is the current screen. Please review it from a designer's point of view, and analyze it in terms of "Is the important information obvious enough?", "Is the spacing too cramped?", and "Is it easy to tap on a phone?" When you're done, just tell me your suggestions and reasons. Don't rush to change anything.
The prompt above is built on a few key points:
First tell it what you want it to do, like "review the screen."
Tell it what point of view to analyze from, like "a designer's point of view."
Tell it which aspects you want analyzed, like "Is the important information obvious enough?", "Is the spacing too cramped?", and "Is it easy to tap on a phone?"
Keep it from being overly helpful and changing the screen right away, since you won't necessarily agree with every suggestion.
The whole process still comes back to "setting design constraints you can check," because you need to know what's off about the screen before you can decide what to change.

So once the screens are updated, can you relax? Nope, not yet.
This round of changes actually touched quite a few files, and there's one big principle you have to remember:
Whenever the UI changes, features might break.
Because of that principle, there's one thing you need to have the AI do: regression testing.
What does that mean? It's simple: retest all the original features one more time to make sure nothing got broken by the layout changes.
There are plenty of ways to do it. You can click through everything yourself:
Add an expense
Enter bad data on purpose
Delete one
Refresh the page
Check that the stats update along with it
Of course, you can also ask the AI to run through all of that for you. This is where you can use Claude in Chrome to have it drive the browser and run the whole set of tests.
Only after everything checks out should you tell the AI something like this and have it commit for you:
Please commit. In the message, say this is a UI improvement and no features changed.
wrapping-up
Wrapping up
That's about it for today, so let's wrap up with a few takeaways.
AI-made screens look "AI-ish" because when you don't give it a direction, it generates screens based on the average of its training data.
Make good use of SKILL extensions, like Frontend Design.
Your prompt doesn't need CSS, but you do need to be able to answer these five questions:
ol
What feel do you want
What absolutely has to be on the screen
What do you hate
How small a screen does it need to work on
What's off-limits
Be specific when tweaking. If you don't know how to describe it, take a screenshot and ask the AI for suggestions.
After a big UI overhaul, you have to do regression testing: run through the features again to make sure nothing got broken.
That's it for today. See you tomorrow!
